div.title: A. Judean hill country.
1. Jerusalem and its surroundings from the west-northwest. V. 775.
div.p: FA 304, No. 18. 22 November 1917, 11 a.m.; altitude 2,500 m; focal length 25 cm.

Jerusalem lies in the center of the picture, its Temple Mount standing out as a bright surface in the midday sun. Because of the altitude from which the photograph was taken, it is not immediately apparent that the terrain beyond the city falls away and that the watershed between the Mediterranean and the Dead Sea runs across the landscape. Yet the valleys before the centerline of the picture descend toward the foreground, that is, westward, while those beyond it run toward the other side, showing that the land falls away there. The surface of the Dead Sea visible in the east lies 390 m below sea level. The highest visible points are the Mount of Olives (815 m) and, on this side of Jerusalem, the height along the Jaffa road (819 m); Jerusalem, descending to 740 m, therefore lies on a surface sloping eastward.

Of the valleys, the principal one is Wadi Lifta in the left foreground, conspicuous for its white channel. Wadi Umm el-‘Amad joins it from the watershed as an eastern tributary. The main valley's farther course, no longer visible here, receives all the other valleys in the lower-right half of the picture: first Wadi ‘Akbet el-Beda toward the foreground, then Wadi ‘En Rauwas to the right, and higher up Wadi Ka‘at el-Uzir. The plain of el-Bak‘a (the Valley of Rephaim, Josh. 15:8) also belongs to this western slope. All of it lies in the basin of Wadi es-Sarar, which drains into the Mediterranean.

Beyond the watershed, Wadi en-Nar, perhaps the Valley of Acacias (John 4:18; compare PJB 1909, p. 13), is the defining feature of Jerusalem's immediate surroundings. Its western tributary, Wadi er-Rababe (the Valley of Ben-Hinnom), appears as a deep channel south of Jerusalem. Wadi en-Nar can be followed first southeastward and then, after a sharp turn eastward, as far as Mar Saba. Wadi Abu Hindi crosses the mountainous desert from west to east and breaks through the mountain chain toward the Dead Sea at the left edge of the picture; Wadi es-Sikke runs parallel to it nearer the watershed. Farther down the descent toward the Dead Sea, the plain of el-Ibke‘a separates the Muntar range from the marginal mountains of the Dead Sea, which stand only about 200 m above Mediterranean sea level. The Dead Sea is visible from the region of ‘En Jidi (Engedi) in the south to its northern end, though the photograph's lack of sharpness makes it indistinguishable from the Jordan Valley. Beyond it rises the plateau of Moab, approximately from Mount Nebo in the north to the Arnon in the south.

Besides Jerusalem, its suburbs to the north, west, and south, and its outlying settlements to the south, the following places are visible. In the foreground is Lifta-Nephtoah (Josh. 15:9), perhaps once situated on the height between the two roads; its spring on the slope to the right of the village sends a small stream into the valley in spring. Deir Yasin is in the right corner. In the northeast, at upper left, is el-‘Isawije (Laisa, Isa. 10:30); et-Tur is on the Mount of Olives; farther east is el-‘Azarije (Bethany, Matt. 21:17; Ananiah, Neh. 11:32, according to Albright), with Abu Dis above it to the right. Sur Bahir is barely recognizable in the southeast. Also visible in the southwest, from left to right, are the Monastery of the Cross and the patriarchal residence at Katamon.

Important roads: From Jerusalem toward the foreground, northwestward, runs the western or Jaffa road. In front, its older southern line forms a switchback in Wadi ‘Akbet el-Beda; higher up, a southern branch leads to ‘En Karim. At left center is the northern or Nablus road, with a bend on the slope of Ras el-Mescharif (Mount Scopus), and above it the Mount of Olives road built in 1898. At the foot of the Mount of Olives, then curving around it twice to the right, is the eastern or Jericho road, which disappears into Wadi es-Sikke. On the right is the southern or Hebron road on this side of the watershed; before it, in Wadi Ka‘at el-Uzir, is the unmetalled southwestern road to Gaza.

The photograph presents a view approximately 30 km wide in the background, about 4 km wide in the foreground, and 40 km deep. It therefore shows a substantial section of the Judean hill country and its desert in a way that even a view from the Mount of Olives cannot. Only someone familiar with the terrain, however, would know that the Mount of Olives range rises rather than falls from the Mount of Olives toward the left edge of the picture.

div.title: 2. Jerusalem and its surroundings from the southeast.
div.p: FA 302, No. 60. 23 November 1917, around noon; altitude 3,000 m; focal length 21 cm. Arrow points northeast.

In the foreground is the Mount of Olives range with its eastern slope. On the left it is bounded by Wadi en-Nar and its two upper branches: to the north, Wadi Silwan and Wadi es-Sitt Mirjam (the Kidron Valley); from the west, Wadi er-Rababe (the Valley of Ben-Hinnom, Josh. 15:8); in front, Wadi Kaddum, a northern tributary of Wadi en-Nar coming from the Mount of Olives; and on the left, Wadi Jasul coming from the watershed.

Beyond Jerusalem is the great valley system of Wadi Bet Hanina, or Wadi Lifta, formed by the two branches Wadi ed-Damm on the right and Wadi Duwed on the left, whose upper course can be followed beyond Rafat. Toward the foreground is its eastern tributary Wadi Umm el-‘Amed; farther to the right are the northern tributaries Wadi ‘Isa and Wadi Buwaj. In the upper background to the right are the valleys around Beit Ur el-Foka (Upper Beth-Horon), and to the left the valleys beyond Kiryat Abu Rosh (Kiriath-Jearim). They belong to the basin of Nahr el-‘Oja, whose watershed is formed by the heights from el-Kerje to Biddu.

The elevations on this side of Jerusalem appear in sequence: Baten el-Haua (727 m), et-Tur (the Mount of Olives, 815 m), Umm et-Tala‘ (818 m), el-Madbase, Ras Abu Halawi, Ras el-Mescharif (Mount Scopus, 779 m), and then the watershed heights as far as Tell el-Ful (840 m). Beyond Jerusalem to the west is the height of Deir Yasin, above it the height of Qastal (808 m), the heights near Kiryat Abu Rosh (763 m), and in the northwest the towering mountain of en-Nebi Samwil (895 m).

Jerusalem's position at the confluence of the Kidron and Ben-Hinnom valleys, the eastward slope of its surface, the southern spur of the Temple hill as an apparent eastern fore-terrace of the western hill, and the southern portions of the western and eastern city hills left outside Jerusalem since the Roman Aelia Capitolina are all clearly visible.

Other settlements: Silwan in the Kidron Valley; et-Tur and the Russian tower on the Mount of Olives; el-‘Azarije (Bethany) in two parts, the older western and younger eastern parts, on the eastern slope; el-‘Isawije (Laisa) east of Mount Scopus; Sho‘fat to the northwest; and Beit Hanina still farther northwest. Above the V in “V. B.” is Bir Nebala; by the r in “Nr.” is ed-Dschib (Gibeon), with en-Nebi Samwil on its height. Above Wadi ‘Isa is Beit Iksa; beyond Wadi Buwaj is Beit Surik, shown dark, with Biddu on the height opposite it. Lifta is hidden behind its height, but above the valley on the far slope is Qalunya, with Deir Yasin on the near side; Qastal is barely recognizable on its height, Beit Nakuba lies farther west, and Kiryat Abu Rosh (Kiriath-Jearim) is in shadow. The Monastery of the Cross, the Templer Colony, and the houses of Deir Abu Tor lie southwest and south of Jerusalem.
In the foreground, the carriage road to Jericho circles south of the principal summit of the Mount of Olives; a shortcut crosses the height above Bethany.

Historically important routes across the Mount of Olives range are: first, a route over the Mount of Olives, passing north of Bethany to the Jericho road; second, a route farther north over the Mount of Olives through Wadi el-Lehham to the Jericho road; and third, the Roman road from the northeastern corner of the city past Umm et-Tala‘, likewise toward Jericho.

The modern road to the Mount of Olives partly follows an old connection to the northern road, which can be traced as far as Ras Abu Halawi. The northern road, with its bends across Wadi ed-Dschoz and on the slope of Ras el-Mescharif, is visible as far as its western fork, the Beth-Horon road, near Tell el-Ful (Gibeah of Saul). The branch of the road toward Jeba‘ is also recognizable; see PJB 1916, p. 54.

The western road shows the southern branch toward ‘En Karim and the older southern secondary line mentioned under No. 1. Beyond Qalunya it climbs, with a bend, to the Qastal pass; farther on, the section from Wadi Ekbala to Kiryat Abu Rosh is visible. The southwestern road to Gaza can be followed, with its branch toward ‘En Karim, as far as the vicinity of the Monastery of the Cross. The southern road is visible only as far as the Templer Colony because an airplane wing conceals the remainder.

The photograph spans about 15 km across the background and surveys a distance of about 18 km: the entire Judean ridge around Jerusalem as far as the beginning of the western descent toward the hill country, the Shephelah, and the coastal plain.

div.title: 3. Jerusalem from the northeast. V. 776. Reichsarchiv.
div.p: FA 300, No. 1334. Photograph taken at about 9 a.m.; deepest shadow to the north.

The view surveys Jerusalem in relation to its eastern valley, the Kidron, its southern valley, Ben-Hinnom, and its southwestern surroundings. In the left foreground is the Mount of Olives with the Ascension shrine (2, 3i); to the right is the Mount of Olives road, beside it the turreted hospice of the Empress Augusta Victoria Foundation (6, 7m). Beyond the Kidron Valley is the walled Old City with the Temple Mount (7–12h), the Church of the Redeemer (13g), the Church of the Holy Sepulchre (14g), the Tower of David (13g), the Franciscan monastery and Christian Brothers' building (16g), and the French hospice (17g). To the south are the Church of the Dormition (9f) and Nebi Daud (8f); beyond them to the west is the Jewish colony (10, 11f), and to the south the houses of Jebel Deir Abu Tor (5, 6f). In the nearer background is the plain of el-Bak‘a, the Valley of Rephaim, draining through the valley of Bettir (13–17c) toward the Mediterranean.

The watershed hills separating the plain from the vicinity of Jerusalem appear low in the west, while the mountains in the background appear enormous. They rise first along the Kremzan ridge (4b–14c) to 900 m, then near Sherifet en-Nebi Danjan (1a) to 994 m. Behind them is the western slope of the Judean hill country.

Settlements: on the height, Beit Jala (1–3b) opposite Bethlehem; beside the plain to the south, Beit Safafa (7d) and Sharafat (9, 10c); to the north, el-Malha (16, 17d), with Bettir probably above it (16c).

Roads: southward, the Hebron road (1d–9f), whose continuation appears again near Sherifet en-Nebi Danjan (1a); in the Kidron Valley, the Jericho road (14i–1h) and the Roman road to Jericho (15i, 16–7l). For the railway line (7, 8e) in the Valley of Rephaim, compare Nos. 7 and 8.

div.title: 4. Jerusalem and its suburbs. View toward the east-southeast. V. 779.
div.p: FA 303, No. 779. 2 November 1917, 8:45 a.m.; altitude 1,800 m.

In the center is the Old City with the Temple Mount, the white Church of the Redeemer (8f), the two domes of the Church of the Holy Sepulchre (9f, left), the Tower of David (6ef), the Austrian Hospice (11g) on the Via Dolorosa, the site of the Antonia Fortress (11h), St. Anne's Church, and the Pool of Bethesda (13i).
Outside the Old City to the south is the Church of the Dormition (2f); to the west is the Sultan's Pool (2, 3ef), with the Montefiore colony and the olive groves of en-Nikeforije above it.

In the west is the Jaffa Gate (7e). Radiating southwestward from it is the road to el-Malha (1a); branching westward from that is the road to ‘En Karim (5a), and northwestward is the road to Jaffa (11a). Between the Jaffa road and the Malha road is the Mamilla Pool (7c), and along the Jaffa road is the Jaffa suburb.

In the north is the Damascus Gate (11, 12f). From there a connecting road leads to the Jaffa road (11a); the northern road passes the church of the Anglican bishop (16, 17e), with connections from there to the northwestern corner of the city (8d) and the southern road. Herod's Gate (14g) has a connecting road to the northern road (17e). At the northeastern corner of the city is Burj Laklak (16i), with the road to Jericho (12m).
In the south is David's Gate, with a path to the Kidron Valley (8m). In the valley are the Virgin's Spring, Gihon (3m), and the Greek Chapel of St. Stephen (12l).

The elevation generally rises toward the northwest and west: the Temple Mount is about 740 m, and the Jaffa road at 11a is 815 m. The valley to the west, containing the Sultan's Pool, and the ridge beyond it are not recognizable as such.

div.title: 5. Old Jerusalem. View toward the southeast. V. 790.
div.p: Photograph taken in the afternoon, with shadows on the eastern slopes.

This vertical photograph gives a clear view into Jerusalem's street system, which is connected with the system of Roman Aelia on the Madaba mosaic. From the Damascus Gate (15a), a market street runs directly south across the city, ending at 6e. A second street goes from the same place first southeastward, then turns south at 13d and, after several bends, reaches the eastern south gate, Bab el-Magharibe (8h). Both lines are crossed by David Street, which runs from the Jaffa Gate (8a) to the Temple platform (11g). Its line corresponded to the northern wall of the city of Jerusalem in Jesus' time. A second cross street begins at 11a and joins the second longitudinal street at 13d. One may then go northwest along this street for a short distance and turn east at the Austrian Hospice (14c), thus reaching St. Stephen's Gate (17h).

The Via Dolorosa begins on the last-mentioned line at the site of the Antonia Fortress (15e), continues along that section of the street from the Damascus Gate, and runs on the second cross street to 12b, where it ends opposite the Church of the Holy Sepulchre as the site of Golgotha (11ab).

The suburb in Jesus' time probably had its western wall along the line of the market street, and its northern wall roughly along the line of the Via Dolorosa. Outside it, then, remained the Church of the Holy Sepulchre, which in Constantine's time had its entrance from the market street, and the so-called Pool of Hezekiah (9ab). The Greek market (10b) is on the site of the Hospital of the Knights of St. John; east of it is the Church of the Redeemer (11c).
Beside the Jaffa Gate is the citadel (7, 8a) with the Tower of David, Psephinos, at the northern boundary of the former palace of Herod, and the barracks square (7ab).

Outside to the south are the Church of the Dormition (3d) and the Cenacle, with David's tomb according to later tradition (4e, lower left), surrounded on three sides by the cemeteries of the Christian denominations.

The approximate course of the southern city wall in Jesus' time ran from 1e to 2l, then turned north on the dam closing the Tyropoeon Valley at 3l, and continued along the edge of the hill to the southeastern corner of the Temple platform (11l). On the slope is the presumed Church of the Repentance of Peter (3g).

By the Kidron is the Virgin's Spring, Gihon, at 8l; the outlet of the rock-cut channel from there is by the Pool of Siloam (4k), and David's fortress of Zion was in the area of 5 and 6k. The Hebron road crosses the dam of the Sultan's Pool in the west at 1ab.

div.title: 6. The Temple platform and Jerusalem. View toward the east-southeast.
div.p: Photograph taken at midday.

Taken from closer range, this oblique photograph has a more three-dimensional effect than the vertical photograph in No. 5. The Haram, which corresponds to the sanctuary of the Herodian period, shows the broad area of the Temple's outermost court (1k–16m), with the al-Aqsa Mosque (2–4lm) above an ancient approach to the Temple; the higher terrace (7km–11im, 12lm), the site of the innermost Temple court, with its eight approaches; the Dome of the Rock (8, 9kl) on the site of the altar; the Dome of the Chain (9l); the rocky northwestern corner of the platform (12–14hi), above which part of the Antonia Fortress stood; the barracks (14, 15i), corresponding to the other part of the fortress; and the pool Birket Isra'in (16lm), which has been regarded as the Pool of Bethesda.

The traditional Via Dolorosa begins at the Antonia Fortress. The Chapel of the Taking Up of the Cross (15g), the Ecce Homo Chapel (14f), and the Ecce Homo Arch (14g) over the street; the junction of the Via Dolorosa with the road from the Damascus Gate (16b); the westward continuation from the corner at 12e in the direction of 9a; the Church of the Holy Sepulchre with two domes (8ab); the German Church of the Redeemer (6, 7c) with its cloister on the left; the Greek market, where the Hospital of the Order of St. John once stood (5, 6bc); the present German Hotel Fast, “St. John” (7b); the Patriarch's Pool (4, 5a); the citadel with the Tower of David, Psephinos (1, 2a), on the site of Herod's fortress; David Street from the Jaffa Gate (3a) to the Temple platform (6i); beside it the courthouse, el-Mehkame (5i), probably the town hall in Jesus' time; and the Jews' Wailing Place (4i) below the enclosure wall of the Temple platform.

The presumed historical Passion route of Jesus led from Herod's palace, the Tower of David, to Golgotha as the opposite height (7–9a-c), outside the suburb wall along the line of the market street (4–10d). The present city wall is 13a–16b, and the road outside it is 14a–16b. Compare Orte und Wege Jesu3, pp. 286ff.

div.title: 7. Jerusalem's southern surroundings. View toward the southeast. V. 784.
div.p: FA 304, No. 2245. 13 July 1918, 6:30 a.m.; altitude 400 m; focal length 50 cm.

An autumn morning picture with shadows to the west. In the foreground the watershed runs approximately along the line of the road from 12f to 5m. East of it is the descent to Wadi en-Nar; west of it is the Valley of Rephaim, whose northern edge begins approximately along the line of the road from 6e to 9e. Here hilly terrain begins, recognizable as rocky by its lighter color and white patches. One high point is the patriarchal seat Katamon (1e, 2d); a valley, Wadi Ka‘at el-Uzir, lies on the line of the road to el-Malha (10d to 1d), with tributaries coming from the north, in the easternmost of which is the Monastery of the Cross (6c). To the right is Jerusalem with the Jaffa suburb, the Old City encircled by the Valley of Ben-Hinnom (13f–16h), above which is the Sultan's Pool (13, 14f).

The Hebron road (13f–1k) has almost parallel secondary lines on both sides with the same destination; a third road (11f–1g) runs through the plain in the direction of Beit Safafa. Of greater importance is the already mentioned road to el-Malha (13d–1d), which may be regarded as the old connection to the southern coastal land and Gaza, and finally the Jaffa road (14d–9a). At the station (12f) the railway from Jaffa arrives; it first follows the Beit Safafa road (1g–5g) and then turns in a curve, passing over 11g, toward the station. Noteworthy is the connecting line through the olive groves of Nikeforiye (13d–12f) between the Malha road and the western Hebron road, now also leading to the station. The new water pipeline built in 1918 appears as a dark line (1h, 5g, 6c, 8a) from the ‘Arrub pool halfway to Hebron; see Nos. 11 and 37 and PJB 1921, pp. 77ff. The new Jewish colony Talpioth lies between the Hebron road and its southern parallel (10h–8i).

div.title: 8. Jerusalem's southern suburb with the German Colony. View toward the northwest. V. 806a.
div.p: FA 304, No. 1411. 20 May 1918, 1:30 p.m.; altitude 5,000 m; focal length 50 cm.

A midday picture with northern shadows. The terrain lies at the point where the Valley of Ben-Hinnom turns from north-south to west-east. The Sultan's Pool, with its small surface of water (2, 3h), fills the valley floor shortly before the turn, followed by a Jewish colony (4f). Olive plantations lie farther below (3d–1b), and more extensively in the area to the west, in the foreground. The Monastery of St. Onuphrius and Hakeldama (1a) are on the southern edge of the valley; the rock tomb of the Herodian family is at 3l, above; and the Greek farmstead et-Talabiye (10k) is in the west.

The so-called Mount Zion in the north, with the group of houses at Nebi Daud (1ef) and the German-English cemetery (2ef), has opposite it, to the west, Jewish colonies (4h–2k); to the south Jebel Abu Tor, the Hill of Evil Counsel (3a–6c); to the southwest the rocky summit Ras ed-Dabbus (6ef), over which the watershed bends from north to east; then the station (7ef), the German Templer Colony (8f–10d–11f), and the leper home of the Protestant Moravian Brethren (13k–14l). Below is the English sports ground (16, 17h).

Historically, the area is significant because the boundary between the tribes of Judah and Benjamin ascended here from the Valley of Ben-Hinnom to the mountain north of the Valley of Rephaim and then turned northeast toward the spring of Nephtoah (Josh. 15:8f.), and because Pompey camped here in 65 BC on Jebel Abu Tor (Jewish War V.12.2). A village called “Kichererbsenhausen” probably occupied Ras ed-Dabbus at that time (Jewish War, same passage).

div.title: 9. Jerusalem's inner western suburb. View toward the east. V. 799.
div.p: FA 304, No. 1354. 18 May 1918, 3:45 p.m.; altitude 4,500 m; focal length 50 cm.

In the center is the Mamilla Pool (8, 9h), the collector of rainwater from the surrounding depression, with which the Valley of Ben-Hinnom is connected, still filled now in May. It is surrounded by a Muslim cemetery, around which traffic must find its way. From the northeastern corner of the Old City, near 11m, the Jaffa road runs to 15a; along it are the small city garden (12l) and the Russian Compound with its church (13, 14i), pilgrims' houses, and administrative buildings (12k–13g–15k), now used for other purposes. Set apart is Talitha Kumi, the girls' orphanage of the Kaiserswerth deaconesses (11b–13b). The connecting road from the Jaffa road to the Damascus Gate (16a–17m) has beside it the hospital of the London Jewish Mission (16, 17a), the German consulate (16bc), the German hospital of the Kaiserswerth deaconesses (15, 16d), and the German Protestant parsonage (17gh). Set apart are the domed Ethiopian church (17f) and the former house of the German Protestant Palestine Institute (17f, left), the American Palestine Institute (17f, below), and the chapel of the English church mission (16kl).

Far to the west are the Ratisbonne school for Arab children (7ab) and the Jewish Bezalel School of Arts and Crafts (9a). By the Mamilla cemetery is the old hospice of the Catholic German Association of the Holy Land (11e). On the left is the road to el-Malha (9m–1c), with a connecting road to the station (8k–1m) through Nikeforiye with military tent camps, and the road to ‘Ain Karim, first toward the Monastery of the Cross (4f–2a). In the area of the Mamilla Pool one may locate the Fuller's Field, on whose road, and also at the starting point of the conduit from the upper pool, Isaiah was to meet King Ahaz (Isa. 7:3). The “Camp of the Assyrians” belongs in the area of the Russian Compound (2 Kings 19:35); Titus too set up the camp there from which he conquered Jerusalem (Jewish War V.3.5; V.12.2).

div.title: 10. Jerusalem's outer western suburb. View toward the southeast. V. 800a.
div.p: FA 304, No. 2588. 1 August 1918, 12:30 p.m.; altitude 4,500 m; focal length 50 cm.

The upper-right corner of picture 9 is repeated here in the lower center. The Jaffa road and the connecting road from the Damascus Gate meet at 8g. Talitha Kumi (7l), the German parsonage (15m), the hospital (11k), the consulate (10i), and the Jewish mission hospital (9, 10gh) are also visible here. New along the Jaffa road are the schools and workshops of the Alliance Israélite (7h) and, far outside, the Jewish Shaare Zedek Hospital (2a). To the right of the Jaffa road and along the left parallel road are Jewish colonies; at 2c and 1d is the Yemenite colony, and the pool Birket el-Khandak is at 1hi. Jewish colonies also lie to the north and east, and the Jewish von Lämel School is at 11g.

A depression that drains eastward through Wadi Lukka toward the upper course of the Kidron Valley corresponds to the northern road parallel to the Jaffa road (10a–17h). On its right side lies the property of Pastor Schneller's Syrian Orphanage, founded in 1860, though the orphanage itself is no longer visible; on the height is “Abraham's Vineyard,” an English Christian foundation for Jewish workers (11, 12a–12, 13b), and beyond it the Jewish Bukharan Colony (15–17g–16d).

Everything west of Jerusalem was without houses until 1859. Only from then on did Christian institutions, and then especially Jewish immigrants, begin to settle the terrain along the Jaffa road. Grain fields and olive groves, in which tents were pitched for summer recreation, and individual watchtowers securing the road accompanied the pilgrim coming from Jaffa as far as the city gate. David too traveled this road when he brought the Ark of God to his city (2 Sam. 6:12); compare PJB 1913, p. 36; 1921, pp. 95, 103.

div.title: 11. The entire western suburb of Jerusalem. View toward the northwest. V. 787.
div.p: FA 304, No. 2941. 15 September 1918, 8 a.m.; altitude 5,000 m; focal length 50 cm.

This view reaches even farther west than No. 10, showing the western suburb from the outside. Here the Jaffa road begins in the area of its greatest height, 819 m (11k), north of which the ground reaches its highest point at 828 m (9k). The watershed between the Mediterranean and the Dead Sea runs as far as this point, because the shallow depression that continues from here over Wadi Lukka toward 1c is connected with the Kidron Valley.

On the north the watershed line follows past the Syrian Orphanage (5h) (formerly Khirbet Bedr) and Abraham's Vineyard (4h), running toward the Karm el-Ka‘k north of Jerusalem (see No. 12). On the south it follows the Jaffa road as far as the former government hospital (7e) and encircles the Mamilla cemetery (7, 8, 9a) on the west and south. The valley of Wadi esh-Sheikh, which runs down from the Jaffa road (10i) to the Monastery of the Cross (16a), already belongs to the descent toward the Mediterranean. The water conduit from the ‘Arrub pools (compare Plate 7) climbs up it to its settling basin (9i) and carries the water from this high point into the city.

The ridge with the tomb of Sheikh Bedr (12i) bounds this valley on the west; beyond it adjoins Wadi Sahyun, which likewise runs northward and along whose western side the road to ‘Ain Karim passes by. Where this road branches off from the Jaffa road (12k), Jewish old-age homes (12kl) and a Jewish asylum (12k) stand beside it.

Olives on the height of Sheikh Bedr and in the valley by the Monastery of the Cross (16ab), young pine plantations near the Syrian Orphanage (4, 5g), and others on the slope of Ras en-Nadir (5l) are important representatives of the tree life in the west of Jerusalem. The pool Birket el-Khandak (11de) collects only rainwater. For the relief of the landscape compare Plate 1.

div.title: 12. Northwest of Jerusalem. View toward the southeast. V. 801.
div.p: FA 304, No. 2944. 15 September 1918, 8:30 a.m.; altitude 5,000 m; focal length 50 cm.

A morning view that links No. 11 with No. 13. The seemingly level area in the center is crossed by the watershed, which, coming from the Syrian Orphanage, runs across this area roughly through its middle and passes over toward the height of the Karm el-Ka‘k (16e). To the north the ground slopes down toward Wadi Umm el-‘Amad (no longer visible), to the south toward the basin of the pool Birket en-Nka‘ (9, 10l) and the upper course (10l, 11m) of Wadi ed-Joz that passes north of it — that is, once again, part of the Kidron Valley.

The land here, used for farming, was once important — especially along the northern slope — because of the burial chambers that were cut into these rocky edges (e.g. 8a, 7ab). On the left is the handsomely laid-out colony of the Bukharan Jews (3d–4h); south of it are more densely built Jewish colonies, of which Mea Shearim (Meshorim), on the road coming from the Syrian Orphanage (2l, 3m), is the best known. Beyond the depression are the outermost groups of houses of the northern suburb, here too a Yemenite colony (10m).

The northern road out of Jerusalem (11m–17i) crosses the valley on an embankment (11m), then climbs steeply (12l, 13k), a stretch that a switchback bypasses to the east (13m). Across the level ground comes from the north (7a) the road from Bet Hanina, ed-Jib–Gibeon, and Nebi Samwil; at 7d it divides into the routes to the Damascus Gate (6m) and to Herod's Gate (9m), with the footpath from Sho‘fat (16a–9l) being less important. Apart from the grounds of the Syrian Orphanage (1, 2b-d) and Abraham's Vineyard (1ef), and a few gardens, there is hardly a tree in the whole area.

div.title: 13. Jerusalem's northern suburb. View toward the south. V. 796.
div.p: FA 304, No. 2945. 15 September 1918, 8:30 a.m.; altitude 5,000 m; focal length 50 cm.

Fairly level ground adjoins the Old City on the north. Yet the ascent toward the watershed in the west (1g-l) is followed by a shallow depression (3, 4k), then the beginning, at 778 m, of Jerusalem's eastern hill — artificially separated by the city wall from its southern continuation (6, 7k). Now called es-Sahira, it was held by Thenius and others to be Golgotha (5–7h), and is famous for the supposedly genuine Tomb of Christ on its western edge (5h). After a second depression (8h) comes a second low rise, the Karm esh-Sheikh (10, 11h), before the descent to the Kidron Valley. This valley (14m, 15d, 10a) encircles the northern suburb on the east and northeast and receives a tributary from the north (12a-c). There are larger stands of olives in various places — gone since the war at 3ef — and a large pine in the Karm esh-Sheikh (10h).

From the Damascus Gate (5k) runs the northern road; east of it stand the German Catholic St. Paul's Hospice (5k), the French Dominican monastery (5, 6fg), the church of the English bishop (5c), and the main house of the “American Colony” (6a). Roads lead to the Jaffa Gate (5c–1e) and to Herod's Gate (5b–8i), beside which is the tomb of the royal family of Adiabene (5, 6b); roads toward Bet Hanina, see No. 12 (2a–4e, 4a–5b); to ‘Anata–Anathoth (12i–16a); the road to Jericho (12i–13m); and the road from the Damascus Gate to the Jaffa road (5k–1g), compare Nos. 9 and 11.

Together with Nos. 9–12, this picture amounts to a plan of the northern and western suburbs of Jerusalem of a kind not previously available. Not only the exact position of every road, but every individual property, is rendered clearly and with complete reliability.

div.title: 14. North and northwest of Jerusalem. View toward the northeast. V. 788.
div.p: FA 304, No. 958. 21 April 1918, 8 a.m.; altitude 4,000 m; focal length 25 cm.

The picture surveys the entire western and northern suburb from the north wall onward (1d-g): the Jaffa road as far as the Jewish old-age homes beyond the watershed (1d–9a), and the northern road (1f–16m) to just short of Sho‘fat, about 3½ km. New here is the ground north of the Karm el-Ka‘k (10h), above all Ras el-Mesharif with its western spur (10l–12i), 779 m high, where the watershed crosses over to the east and then continues northward.

At it begins Wadi Umm el-‘Amad (13h–17d), which empties into Wadi Bet Hanina (Lifta) (17c–14a). Cloud shadows darken its southern slopes and hang over the suburb. In its full length the valley appears below the Syrian Orphanage (10c–15b).

Not everywhere distinct is the road to Bet Hanina (4f–16e), beside which lies the so-called Tomb of the Judges (11e), and its branch toward Bet Iksa (11d–16b); entirely clear are the northern road with its switchback at Ras el-Mesharif and the fork toward Jeba‘ (14m), and the Mount of Olives road with its shortcut (6i-m) leading to ‘Anata, like the road from the corner of the city (1i–4m).

div.title: 15. The Mount of Olives range. View toward the north. V. 836.
div.p: FA 304, No. 1524. 26 May 1918, 1 p.m.; altitude 4,500 m; focal length 50 cm.

The Mount of Olives is the southernmost peak of a ridge running first to the southeast and then to the south, as the Mount of Olives road indicates (17i–10c). The mountain itself divides into the Ascension summit (815 m), with the Ascension shrine and the village of et-Tur (10bc); the Russian summit (818 m), with the Russians' tall bell tower (8, 9c); and the Galilee summit (813 m), with a Greek church for the event of Matt. 28:16ff. (11, 12d). After a slight dip in the ridge there follow, to the north, the German summit — Arabic Umm et-Tala‘ (813 m) — with the hospice of the Empress Augusta Victoria Foundation (9, 10g), and the Jewish summit — Arabic el-Madbase (831 m) — which is to carry the Hebrew University (14k).

East of the Russian summit adjoins the much lower Ras esh-Shiyah, now settled again (5, 6b). Together with the Mount of Olives ridge, the eastern fall of the Russian summit forms the watershed between Wadi en-Nar and Wadi es-Sidr. To the basin of the former belong Wadi Kaddum (5a–7b) in the south and the Kidron Valley (12a–17f) in the west, while the eastern valleys belong to the basin of Wadi es-Sidr — more precisely, as far as Umm et-Tala‘ to Wadi el-Lehham (3a–1h), and then as far as el-Madbase to Wadi Merajir ed-Daba‘. The small plain of Ibke‘dan (1ik) thus belongs to the latter. Ras et-Tmim (probably 2lm) has lately been proposed as Bahurim.

The important routes, besides the carriage road up the Mount of Olives, are the carriage road to Jericho (17d–1b), which skirts the mountain on the south, and then three paths leading over the ridge to the same destination. The first passes over the Ascension summit, by the Bethphage chapel (6c), and runs either by way of el-‘Azarije–Bethany (1a) or directly (1b) to the Jericho road. The second crosses the Mount of Olives south of the Ascension summit (10c) and reaches the carriage road along Wadi el-Lehham (1f). The third, once a Roman road, skirts Umm et-Tala‘ on the south (10f) and joins the carriage road only halfway to Jericho. For Jesus' road from Jericho to Jerusalem all three must be considered; the northernmost is the most likely.
For the relief of the Mount of Olives ridge compare No. 2, and Orte und Wege Jesu3, fig. 30 (an aerial view of the Mount of Olives ridge from the east).

div.title: 16. The Mount of Olives and the Kidron Valley. View toward the southeast. V. 792.
div.p: FA 304, No. 1357. 18 May 1918, 3:15 p.m.; altitude 4,500 m; focal length 50 cm.

On the Mount of Olives are visible the Ascension summit, with the round Ascension shrine (14kl) and the Carmelite convent (13l) with the Pater Noster shrine (12k), and the Galilee summit (17h-k). The western slope shows its three paths to Jerusalem: the northern one, with its bend at the so-called Tombs of the Prophets (10k), probably once continuing straight toward the Bethphage chapel; the middle one, at the site of Jesus' Weeping (Luke 19:41) (12h); and the southern one, which now bends up toward the Ascension summit (15k), but originally continued over the saddle between the Ascension and Galilee summits and also offered a connection to the Roman road (see No. 15).

The Franciscan garden of Gethsemane lies near the foot of the mountain (11, 12d), with the site of the now-rebuilt old church beside it on the south; above it is the Russian Church of Mary Magdalene (11f), below it the Tomb of the Virgin (12d) and the Grotto of the Agony (12d). The Jericho road crosses the valley floor here (12d) and then runs along the near side of it, over the bare slope covered with Jewish gravestones.

In the valley below — formerly planted with olives — are the Tomb of Absalom (8, 9e), the Tomb of St. James and the Tomb of Zechariah (8f), the Spring of the Virgin (formerly Gihon) (3e), and the Arab village of Silwan (1–4gf). Among the routes to the city, note the detour of the carriage road to St. Stephen's Gate (13c–12b), the road to the David Gate (10e–1a), which probably corresponds to an old road, and its former connection to the southern Mount of Olives paths (9ef, 10g). The Golden Gate (10c) of the Temple Mount remains without a direct approach. Compare Orte und Wege Jesu3, pp. 273ff., 338ff.

div.title: 17. The Jericho road I (descent from Bethany). View toward the northeast. V. 844.
div.p: FA 304, No. 216. 3 January 1918, 2:15 p.m.; altitude 3,000 m; focal length 21 cm.

The fall toward the desert from the southern end of the Mount of Olives ridge is broken up by a number of valleys. To the Wadi es-Sidr system belongs Wadi es-Sikke, called Wadi el-Hod in its upper course (8e-m), with its tributaries: on the left Wadi ed-Jemel (5g–7i), on the right Wadi ‘Arak Nazil, or Wadi el-Lehham (13c–9k), which comes from the Mount of Olives, and Wadi Mrajir ed-Daba‘, beginning at the Ibke‘dan depression (15d). From Bethany comes Wadi Abu Dis (9b–1f), which belongs to a second main branch of Wadi es-Sidr. At the edge of the picture Wadi en-Nar is touched (1–6a). From the 818 m of the Mount of Olives the ground falls to el-‘Azarije (615 m) by 200 m, and a further 300 m to the junction of Wadi ed-Jemel with Wadi es-Sikke (about 400 m).
Settlements: el-‘Azarije–Bethany, in two parts (9b), and the history-less Abu Dis (4, 5c), the outermost outposts of the settled land toward the desert.

The Jerusalem–Jericho carriage road can be traced from Wadi Kaddum (11a) over el-‘Azarije to Wadi es-Sikke (8m); besides it, the path over Bethphage to the road (12a–9b), the path through Wadi el-Lehham (13a–12e), the Roman road (15a-c) with a connecting path toward Wadi el-Lehham (14b–13d), and the path from Abu Dis to Jerusalem (5b–8a) as a dark line. — The arrow is inexact.

div.title: 18. Jericho II (the ascent of Adummim). View toward the north. V. 857.
div.p: FA 304, No. 955. 21 April 1918, 8 a.m.; altitude 4,000 m; focal length 23 cm.

In the middle of the desert, at the boundary of the basins of Wadi es-Sidr (16d–8a), of Wadi el-Kelt through its side branch Wadi Abu-d-Dba‘ (5, 6f–4i), and of Wadi Medbah ‘Aijad (4e–1d), which runs parallel to Wadi el-Kelt. The depression of the first step of the hill country's eastern fall ends here at a height of 196 m, after which, with the climb to 310 m at the castle ruin Kal‘at Tal‘at ed-Damm (3f), the second step follows.

The carriage road begins here, 6 km beyond its eastern end on No. 17; it first runs along Wadi es-Sidr (16d–14e), surmounts with switchbacks (on both ascent and descent) at Turret el-Beda the ground swell between it and a tributary (13e–11f), and then passes over into the depression below the height of Kal‘at ed-Damm, which it crosses at Khan Hatrur, the so-called Inn of the Good Samaritan (4f), in order now to descend as the Tal‘at ed-Damm — the ascent of Adummim of Josh. 15:7 — (4e–1f).

The road from ‘Anata–Anathoth joins the carriage-road line at Turret el-Beda (16f–13f); a road from Jeba‘ over Wadi Fara runs somewhat farther east (12i–9g). The Kelt spring is reached by way of Wadi Abu-d-Dba‘ (7f–3i).

div.title: 19. The Jericho road III (Wadi el-Kelt). View toward the southeast. V. 862.
div.p: FA 304, No. 2602. 1 August 1918, 12:20 p.m.; altitude 4,500 m; focal length 50 cm.

The road now descends continuously from its height at Khan Hatrur (1d), 310 m; by the probably still-ruined coffee house Khan el-Meshrab (11g) it is only 131 m high, and at the right edge of the picture (16i), about 5 km from Jericho, 27 m above sea level. To the north it is accompanied by a higher rim that introduces the fall toward Wadi el-Kelt, which — as the deepest channel of the desert in this region — drains the area east of the watershed from Ras Abu Halawi as far as Betin.

The main valley is visible before the confluence of Wadi Fara (from the left) and Wadi es-Sweinit (from the right) at 12b; then follow the area of the spring el-Fauwar (13c), the spring ‘Ain el-Kelt (13e), and the mill driven by its stream (14e), below the mouth of the side valley Wadi Abu-d-Dba‘ coming from the southwest (1c–13e). Above it rises the ridge of ‘Arak Ibrahim (2a–9b), the watershed between Wadi Fara and Wadi Abu-d-Dba‘.

Through the foreground, as a branch of the main road, runs the so-called Nebi Musa road (11g–4m), which since 1908 has provided an easier-to-maintain carriage road to Jericho, at the cost of a 6½ km detour to the south. At its heights the desert appears everywhere covered with the youngest limestone strata (nari). Where the fall to the Jordan plain sets in (6l–16k), erosion has exposed a long band of flint.

div.title: 20. The Jericho road IV (descent to the Jordan Valley). View toward the northeast. V. 1042.
div.p: FA 304, No. 721. 27 March 1918, 3:30 p.m.; altitude 3,000 m; focal length 25 cm.

The road (13a–3m) now runs, at the fracture line of the Jordan rift, already 27 m below sea level, in the immediate vicinity of the water-bearing Wadi el-Kelt, whose monastery lies beyond the upper edge of the picture; and it finally has, despite two switchbacks (11e, 10f), a very steep descent to about −180 m, while Jericho lies another 70 m lower. An old pack trail straight to the Jordan ford by Wadi el-Kelt runs farther south through Wadi Medbah ‘Aijad (7a–1f). Parallel to the mountain fall, the great meridional valley-route runs northward (1e–9m).

A castle ruin is Khirbet Kakun (5f); an old collecting pool for the water led here from the Kelt spring is Birket Musa (5hi). A northern, waterless tributary of Wadi el-Kelt is Wadi Shuchch ed-Daba‘ (16f–9i); on the near side of it begins the ascent (13k–16l) to a historically important road toward Betin (see PJB 1913, pp. 26ff.; 1914, p. 17). Military camps and trenches at various places. Not a tree.

div.title: 21. The northern road from Jerusalem I (Sho‘fat and Tell el-Ful). View toward the northeast. V. 648.
div.p: FA 304, No. 2704. 15 August 1918, 1:30 p.m.; altitude 4,800 m; focal length 50 cm.

Only a few hundred meters are missing from the picture for the road to connect with No. 14. The older line of the road departs little from the new one. Independent of it is a military field railway (1b), which soon crosses the road (6c) and then continues on the other side (as far as 12i).
The watershed follows the heights east of the road. Down to Wadi ed-Damm (17a) runs the two-branched side valley Challet Mesh‘al.

Besides the village of Sho‘fat (4, 5ab), the hill opposite it—occupied by the insignificant ruin Khirbet es-Soma‘ (3f)—is noteworthy, and still more the hill of Tell el-Ful (7k), the ruin of the fortress of Saul's Gibeah. At the eastern foot of this hill runs a path from Hezma to Jerusalem (5m–1e). On the northern road in general see PJB 1925; on Tell el-Ful see Linder, Sauls Gibea (1922), and Albright, Annual IV (1924), pp. 1ff.

div.title: 22. The northern road from Jerusalem II (Bet Hanina, er-Ram). View toward the east-northeast. V. 642.
div.p: FA 304, No. 231. 3 January 1918; altitude 3,000 m; focal length 25 cm.

From the road, 2 cm (1, 2d) repeat about 7 cm of No. 21. There then follow stretches with greater deviations of the new line from the straight-running old one, up to the crossing of Wadi en-Nuss (9b), at which point the old and new lines coincide.
Here too the watershed follows the heights east of the road, from Tlel el-Ful (1de) to the hill of the village er-Ram—Ramah (13m).

The Beth-horon road coming from Jaffa and Lydda (16c–3e) passes the hill of Khirbet ‘Addase—Adasa (14d) and joins the northern road at Khirbet el-Hawanit (3d). Less important is the path from the village of Bet Hanina (8, 9ab) to the main road (3e) and to the Beth-horon road (11e), but important is the way from er-Ram (13m) over Kharaib er-Ram, now a quarry, to the Beth-horon road and Gibeon (16d), with a branch line below er-Ram (12m) from Dscheba—Geba of Benjamin.

— The valley below er-Ram crosses the northern road as Wadi en-Nuss (8h), then runs as Wadi ed-Damm before the area of Bet Hanina (9b) and empties into Wadi Bet Hanina (5a), coming from ed-Dschib—Gibeon, the great water artery of the terrain west of the watershed, here visible at the upper edge of the picture from the area of Bir Nebala (16a) onward. Terraces on the slopes and fields on the flats show the cultivation of the land.

div.title: 23. The northern road from Jerusalem III (Kalandie, Kufr ‘Akab, Rafat). View toward the east. RA.
div.p: FA 301, No. 908. 15 April 1918, 8 a.m.; altitude 4,200 m; focal length 50 cm.

Only about 2 cm are missing for the connection with No. 22. The valley channel of the upper course of Wadi en-Nuss veers off westward in the plain of el-Bak‘a (1f–4e–10h), while the road runs straight on until, at Khirbet ‘Attara—Ataroth-addar (11i), it rejoins the valley and now passes Tell en-Nasbe (15ik) in Wadi Dschiljan.

Present-day settlements are, in the east, Kufr ‘Akab (9i, not at the name), and in the west, Kalandie (6c), Dschedire (6a) and Rafat (13b), the last two in the area of the parallel valley Wadi Bir ed-Der (16a–5a), the upper course of Wadi Bet Hanina.
The valley on the near side of the carriage road (3–1i), with its branches above, belongs to Wadi en-Natuf, a side valley of Wadi es-Swenit, and thus to the catchment of the Jordan.

div.title: 24. The northern road from Jerusalem IV (Tell en-Nasbe). View toward the east. V. 595.
div.p: FA 304, No. 224. 3 January 1918, 2:15 p.m.; altitude 3,000 m; focal length 25 cm.

The road (5½ cm here = 8 cm on No. 3), less distinct, begins at Khirbet ‘Attara—Ataroth-addar (1f), passes the spring ‘En en-Nasbe (4g) and the ancient settlement site of Tell en-Nasbe, probably Mizpah (5f), and reaches as far as near the spring of el-Bire (17g).

To the system of Wadi ed-Damm belong Wadi Dschiljan (17f–1f), in which the road runs, and the parallel Wadi Duwet to the west (according to the English map) (11c–2f), with a path from Ramallah to the carriage road (17d–1f).

The path from el-Bire to Rafat (14f–5a) is important as a connection to the Beth-horon road at el-Latatin. As the upper course of Wadi Bet Hanina may be reckoned the Wadi Bir ed-Der lying still farther west (15b–9a), which the path from Ramallah to ed-Dschib—Gibeon follows.
To the eastern drainage of the country belongs Wadi el-‘En (17g–6i), coming from el-Bire, a tributary of Wadi es-Swenit.

div.title: 25. The northern road from Jerusalem V (el-Bire, Ramallah). View toward the northeast. V. 596.
div.p: FA 304, No. 225. 3 January 1918, 2:15 p.m.; altitude 3,000 m; focal length 25 cm.

From No. 24, 9 cm on the right are repeated here on the left as 7½ cm. The northern road coming from Wadi Dschiljan crosses the height of the watershed (6e, 7f) and passes between the village of el-Bire (8, 9gh), 810 m, and the Ras et-Tahune (11fg), 893 m, over into the region of valleys belonging to the eastern slope of the country (Wadi es-Swenit), while the watershed continues to the west.
Jebel et-Tawil (1–3kl), though at 910 m the highest point of the area, lies on the near side of the watershed.

The northern road continues from 12i as a carriage road in a northerly direction (16i). A second branch, which was probably the oldest northern road, turns from 12i to the northeast (15m) in the direction of Betin—Bethel (14m).

West of el-Bire lies Ramallah (11–12ab), 869 m, connected to it and to the northern road (at 7e) by a road, above the Wadi el-Merara (13d–15b) skirting it to the north, belonging to the system of the Nahr el-‘Odscha. There is, however, also a path running northward along the watershed between Ramallah and el-Bire (7e–17g), whose nearest destinations must be taken to be Surda and Dschifna—Gophna, but which also ties in further connections to the northwest.

div.title: 26. The northern road from Jerusalem VI (the road to Bethel). View toward the east. V. 597.
div.p: FA 304, No. 226. 3 January 1918, 2:15 p.m.; altitude 3,000 m; focal length 25 cm.

About 10 cm to the right of No. 25 equal 9 cm to the left of No. 26. The northern road, remaining always east of the watershed, here passes the great winter water-pond el-Balu‘ (12, 13de), which forms a basin without outflow but nevertheless stands in connection with a valley running off to the east (6k–m) that, like the more southerly Wadi ed-Dscherar (7d–1e), belongs to the system of Wadi es-Swenit.
The pond lies 834 m high and proves that it, and with it the road, lies not much lower than the height reached at el-Bire.

The old northern path leading past Betin—Bethel is visible only as far as the area of ‘En el-Kas‘a (7m). The path running closer to the carriage road toward the southeast (7e–15m) has the village of ‘En Ebrud as its nearest goal and from there makes possible a connection to the line of the carriage road, but also leads past ‘En Ebrud back to the old northern path. — The village of el-Bire appears again at the upper left (2, 3a), beside it the white rock surfaces of its threshing floors (2, 3c).

div.title: 27. The northern road from Jerusalem VII (Bethel—Betin). View toward the east. RA.
div.p: FA 301, No. 909. 15 April 1918, 8 a.m.; altitude 4,200 m; focal length 50 cm.

This picture repeats, in 2½ cm of its upper part, about 3½ cm of the lowest part of No. 26. The watershed of the country, which skirts the pond el-Balu‘ (No. 26) on the west, then turns immediately eastward, crosses over to the north side of the height on whose south ‘En el-Kas‘a lies (5b), and then follows the ridge between two valleys, on which the old northern road of the country (4a–17k) continues.

To the west, Wadi el-Masajat (10a–17g) runs northward, but then turns west toward the system of Wadi Der Ballut and the Nahr el-‘Odscha. In the east, Wadi el-Mesil (17k–1h) runs southward, then joins Wadi ‘Abbas (4a–1f), which comes from the watershed, and unites with the system of Wadi es-Swenit, which belongs to the catchment of the Jordan.

Between the two valleys, separated from the watershed by a hollow running down to Wadi el-Mesil, lies—881 m high—Betin (8–10g), once Bethel, on a low elevation; to its south a pond (7, 8g) with the spring of the place, and to the north a group of natural rock ledges, el-Kal‘at (12–14h), which has sometimes been identified as its ancient sanctuary.

For the location of Bethel it was important that near it an eastern road leading to Jericho branches off from the meridional road of the country. It crosses Wadi el-Mesil in a southeasterly direction and then turns more to the east (9f, 8h, 1m). In doing so it skirts Burj Betin (5k) with the ruins of a church, the presumed site of the ancient sanctuary which, according to Genesis 12:8 and 13:3, lay east of Bethel.

Of local importance is the path to Burka (6–1i). Important, however, is the way through Wadi el-Masajat (9a–17g), later passing ‘En Ebrud, which may be described as a parallel line to the northern road and rejoins it 5 km north of Betin. Cf. Sternberg, ZDPV 1915, pp. 1ff. (see also No. 26).

div.title: 28. Michmash and Wadi es-Swenit. View toward the northeast. V. 638.
div.p: FA 304, No. 221. 3 January 1918, 2:15 p.m.; altitude 3,000 m; focal length 21 cm.

The village of Muchmas (8, 9c), biblical Michmash, lies 607 m high on the eastern slope of the Judaean country above the deeply incised Wadi es-Swenit, which belongs to the catchment of the Jordan. Of this valley only a small loop is visible (5, 6ab). A side branch descending from the height, Wadi et-Tin (17g–7a), determines its position from the south, and Wadi ez-Zetun (13h–1e) with the village's olives from the north—a position on a ridge that is connected with higher ground only in the northwest.
Here too lies its natural connection toward the ridge of the country in the direction of Betin—Bethel, the path recognizable from 10f to 14g.
A northern connection leads past Tell el-‘Askar (9, 10i) toward Rammun. To the southwest there is no lack of a path toward er-Ram (10e–15c).

In a southerly direction the depth of Wadi es-Swenit must be crossed in order to reach, first, Dscheba. The main path (not recognizable) crosses the valley at the mouth of Wadi et-Tin (7a); a second path runs together with the path to er-Ram farther west, but then turns southward. On this see ZDPV 1904, pp. 161ff.; 1905, pp. 161ff.; PJB 1916, p. 48f.

div.title: 29. Ephron-Ephraim-et-Taijibe. View toward the west. V. 581.
div.p: FA 304, No. 1753. 5 June 1918, 7:30 a.m.; altitude 4,800 m; focal length 50 cm.

With the high mountain range of Baal Hazor (el-‘Asur), not visible here, as its backdrop, the Christian village of et-Taijibe—once Ephron and Ephraim—thrones, visible from afar but off the great traffic routes, on its knoll (869 m). In this picture it appears by itself, surrounded north and south by great olive plantations that, on the south, fill Wadi Abul-Haijat (7f–15a). Its own height is the northern termination of a chain of heights that begins at Rammun and has its most prominent summit south of et-Taijibe in the Ras ez-Zemera (16h).
A particular hill in the east, beyond the village's threshing ground, bears the ruin of a three-aisled church (6h), called el-Chadr, which commemorates Jesus' stay in Ephraim (John 11:54).

Past it a path leads to the south (8h–17g), at first toward Rammun, continuing northward toward Der Edschrir and Kufr Malik (9i–1g). The connection to the northern road of Jerusalem is represented by a path to the west (9h–m), and a path to the southeast (4d–12a) by the descent to Jericho.
See Orte und Wege (3rd ed.), pp. 231ff., PJB 1925; cf. Albright, Annual IV, pp. 124ff.

div.title: 29a. The Rock of Rimmon, Rammun. View toward the west. V. 636.
div.p: FA 304, No. 219. 3 January 1918, 2:15 p.m.; altitude 3,000 m; focal length 21 cm.

The image, labeled as Mukhmas, was identified — with the agreement of Professor Albright — as Rammun, which lies 3 km south of et-Taijibe (No. 29) on the road to Mukhmas. It appears to occur as the “Rock of Rimmon” in Judges 20:45 and 21:13, and is recorded as Remmon by Eusebius and on the Madaba map.

The settlement lies at 762 m on a rocky height between the valleys Wadi ed-Dschami‘ (to the west) and Wadi Abu el-Hayat (to the east), both of which run south into Wadi et-Taff, which belongs to the system of Wadi en-Nue‘me (images 72 and 80).

Below the village (12, 13fg) lies a large cave (Shqaf Daher) with a collapsed roof, which one might imagine as the refuge of the Benjaminites in Judges 20–21 (13c), and a rock tomb with the shrine of Sheikh Dschildschal (11, 12c).
The road to et-Taijibe runs 11f–1g; the road to Mukhmas, 13g–17f.

div.title: B. Judean hill and coastal country.
30. The western road from Jerusalem. View toward the southeast. V. 739.
div.p: FA 304, No. 101. 3 December 1917, 1:45 p.m.; altitude 3,200 m; focal length 25 cm.

A late-autumn picture of Judaean landscape in the early afternoon, from the region of Wadi es-Sarar, to which belongs all the land west of the country's watershed, from el-Bire in the north to el-Chadr in the south. The slope at the lower edge of the picture belongs to Wadi Kalonie, a continuation of Wadi Bet Hanina, 6 km west of Jerusalem (cf. No. 2). A considerable ridge separates this valley from Wadi el-Rrab (6b–1a), whose branch is Wadi ‘En Raf‘a (3b–6e), above Wadi Ekbala (7–10f), called Wadi ‘En Dschamil (11g–17h).

The Jerusalem–Jaffa carriage road, which here had sunk to 558 m, has to climb within 1½ km up to 751 m (at 13i), hence the switchbacks at 12, 13m, whose lowest part is missing. The road then drops again to Wadi Ekbala (9f), 614 m, and has a new ascent up to 751 m at Der el-Azhar (8b), where the watershed between the region of Wadi es-Sarar and the Nahr el-‘Odscha begins, whose outermost valleys appear between 7a and 16ab—see especially Wadi Katanne (12–15a).

Settlements: Kastal (11i), Suba (3f), both on towering knolls; Bet Nakuba (10e) above Wadi Ekbala, with the ruin Khirbet Ekbala and the oak grove of Schech ‘Abdallah (7f); Kerjet Abu Rosch—Kirjath Jearim (8b, 9bc) on its slope; el-Amur (3, 4b) above Wadi ‘En Raf‘a, before the latter's confluence with the head of Wadi el-Rrab (6b–1a).

Besides the carriage road, a significant route is the connection—recognizable only at 9–11b—from the carriage road at Kerjet Abu Rosch over Baten es-Sa‘ide (13bc), 877 m, first to Biddu, then via ed-Dschib to el-Bire. Cf. PJB 1913, pp. 35ff.; 1921, pp. 95ff.

div.title: 31. Bethlehem, north. View toward the south-southeast. V. 915.
div.p: FA 304, No. 2269. 13 July 1918, 6:20 a.m.; altitude 4,000 m; focal length 50 cm.

On a ridge connected with the watershed, Bethlehem lies 777 m high between valleys running off toward the east. But toward the west too it appears high, because the upper course of Wadi Ahmed (5a–1e), which runs along the watershed, separates the height of Bethlehem from the ridge of Bet Dschala, whose beginning is visible at 1a.

The Jerusalem–Hebron road (14a–1b) sends out, near Rachel's Tomb (13b), a side branch (12b–10i) that makes the connection with Bethlehem. From Hebron a similar side branch does the same (1–7k). The road to Bet Dschala runs 7h–2a. The old Bethlehem is to be presumed on this side of the line 7–9i.

Prominent buildings: the house of the French teaching brothers (9g), the hospital of the French Sisters of St. Vincent (7gh), the Carmelite convent (3, 4i), the hospital of the Swedish Jerusalem Society (6f), and the Christmas Church (Weihnachtskirche) of the German Jerusalem Society (7i), whose tower is recognizable by its long pointed shadow (morning light).
The cistern before the gate, from which David had water fetched (2 Samuel 23:15), is shown on a northeastern hill spur (12i).

div.title: 32. Bethlehem, south. View toward the southeast. V. 916.
div.p: FA 302, No. 2268. 13 July 1918, 6:30 a.m.; altitude 3,000 m; focal length 50 cm.

About 1½ cm of this picture repeats the previous one, though its direction is not the same. The arrow on both pictures is inaccurate. Old Bethlehem appears here in context (5–7a to d). Adjoining it are the Church of the Nativity (8de) and the southern suburb; all of it between the heads of the valleys—Wadi es-Samur to the east (7b–16i) and Wadi Umm el-Kala to the west (3a–4m)—which later, joined together, run toward the Dead Sea.

Among the routes, the significant ones are the road to Artas (5d–1d), to Khirbet Teku‘-Thekoa (6g·k–4m), and to the nearby Bet Sahur (7d–14m). A composite overall view of Bethlehem (aerial photograph), Orte und Wege3, fig. 3.
Terrain set with olive trees all around the town, on the eastern descent of its own height, in the valleys on both sides, and on the mountains opposite.

div.title: 33. Bethlehem and the Shepherds' Field. View toward the south-southeast. V. 918.
div.p: FA 304, No. 2809. 30 August 1918, noon; altitude 4,400 m; focal length 50 cm.

Bethlehem, south, with the Church of the Nativity (2a) is visible at the upper left. One overlooks the southeast-facing descent of the height of Bethlehem, covered with olive groves, which broadens considerably and then runs out into a plain almost entirely occupied by fields (9bc–16bi). In this plain lies the olive grove of the Shepherds' Field of the tradition associated with Luke 2:8ff. (17fg); at its edge is the village of Bet Sahur (9d–14f).
The road to Thekoa can be followed farther here (as far as 1i). Otherwise noteworthy are the roads to the desert (4i, 17egi) and the road (15a) toward Sur Bahir, lying to the northeast.

The reason for placing the “Shepherds' Field” in the plain below Bethlehem was a flock tower (Migdal Eder) that existed here, which could be understood as protection for the sheep spending the night near the desert. Cf. Orte und Wege3, pp. 49ff.

div.title: 34. The pools and el-Chadr. View toward the northeast. V. 927.
div.p: FA 304, No. 113. 3 December 1917, 1:45 p.m.; altitude 3,200 m; focal length 25 cm.

Immediately beside the Hebron road, 4 km southwest of Bethlehem, lies the strong spring ‘En Salih (9e), whose water Pilate probably first conducted to Jerusalem. Three pools (7h, 8gh), in part only of Arab origin, were meant to store the spring water that was surplus in winter for the summer; an Arab fortress (9h) guarded the important point. But other springs too lie below in the valley. Beside it lay Etam, now Khirbet Wadi el-Choch (5h), and the village of Artas (5i) still lies there, with a South American convent opposite it (4i).

The valley connects here with Wadi el-Bijar coming from the southwest (2b–4h), which through its western side valleys is linked to the country's watershed; the latter, before the road to el-Chadr (15ik) branches off from the Hebron road (10h), rises in a great westward arc to the height of the massif of Scherifet en-Nebi Danjan (994 m), whose summit the picture no longer shows, so that all the valleys in the picture drain to the Dead Sea except the small basin of el-Chadr, which has no outlet. At the foot of the summit of esch-Scherife, at the bend in the road, is the spring ‘En Masur (10a).

Barely recognizable is the old line of the Hebron road, which, beyond the pools near 8g, crosses over the heights to the upper course of Wadi el-Bijar (2a). Small settlements were Khirbet ‘Alja (8f) and Kh. Nustas, or Kh. el-Bire (7c).
The new water pipeline from Wadi ‘Arrub, which crosses the road on this side of the pools, is not visible, because it did not yet exist in December 1917. Later photographs show it clearly.

div.title: 35. Hebron and its immediate surroundings. View toward the northeast. V. 963.
div.p: FA 304, No. 2696. 15 August 1918, 1:30 p.m.; altitude 4,800 m; focal length 50 cm.

Hebron lies in southern Judaea, 927 m high, but—at least as the Arab el-Chalil—it is a settlement of slopes and valley, lying in a valley system that runs by way of Beersheba toward the Mediterranean. It is made up of seven quarters: 1. Harat el-Meschareka (3g); 2. H. el-Kitun (1, 2b); 3. H. el-Haram (3h, 4gh) with the Tombs of the Patriarchs (3h) and the Sultan's Pool (4g) on the valley road; 4. H. el-‘Akkabe and 5. H. el-Kazzazin (5, 6g); 6. H. Bab ez-Zawie (7, 8g) on the road; 7. H. esch-Schech (6h–8gh) on the slope; in addition the extensive northern suburb along the road to Jerusalem (9g–14i).
The olive-covered hill er-Rumede (6–8ef) is probably the site of the Hebron of the Israelite period.

A plain covered with fields and vineyards lies to the northwest, through which run the road (12–16f) to Abraham's Oak and, via Bet Dschibrin, into the coastal land; above it, in a great arc, the carriage road to Beersheba (8f–14a); an older road to the same destination (4g–9a); the southern road to Jatta along Wadi el-Kadi (2g–1b); and the eastern road to Beni Ne‘em and ‘En Dschidi on the Dead Sea (3i–6m).

div.title: 36. Hebron and the southern Judean hill country. View toward the northeast. V. 961.
div.p: Morning photograph.

The city itself appears narrowed and partly concealed by the eastern height, owing to the more oblique photograph. But the view, which in the previous picture reached only as far as the line below e–e, here takes in a large part of the southwestern hill country.

The road to Beersheba can be seen descending into Wadi Sel ed-Dilbe (5c) and, with a long switchback and shortcut, climbing again on the southern slope (7b), passing the summit el-Hadab (891 m) (15a). There is no settlement in this area of about 20 km extent. At the edge of the picture, west-southwest near 7a, Dura-Adoraim (2 Chronicles 11:9) should lie.

In Hebron are the Haram, the sanctuary of the Tombs of the Patriarchs 4k, the hill er-Rumede 6h–9hi, and the vineyards 12c–17i. Its position on the country's great north–south line, the cultivable terrain toward the north, and the mountain spur of er-Rumede are the most important preconditions for David's first capital.

div.title: 37. The pool and pipeline of Wadi ‘Arrub. View toward the west-northwest. V. 951.
div.p: FA 304, No. 2278. 13 July 1918, 6:30 a.m.; altitude 3,000 m; focal length 50 cm.
The road from Hebron to Jerusalem (1i–5m) crosses, 11 km before Hebron, the broad Wadi ‘Arrub, which belongs to the eastern slope of the land. An inn (3i) is a much-used stopping place there.

But the valley gained new importance through the Jerusalem water pipeline laid out in 1918 by the British army administration, which restored the catchment pool (11bc)—probably built in the 14th century—for the valley's springs and gave the water a new course through metal pipes. By machine power the water is pumped from there (830 m), through the pipeline visible in the picture as far as 1i, up to the height north of the valley of Wadi ‘Arrub, to a settling basin lying 940 m high, from which it flows off to Jerusalem.
The old conduit ran off to the east (12a) and, by long routes, reached Jerusalem in a covered channel. Cf. PJB 1921, pp. 77ff.; PEFQ 1919, pp. 15ff.
The level valley floor is well cultivated with fields, unlike the slopes to the sides, on which, toward the road, remnants of oak woodland can also be recognized as short black strokes.

div.title: 38. Descent to the hill country (Bab el-Wad). View toward the north. V. 683.
div.p: FA 304, No. 56. 29 November 1917, 12:30 p.m.; altitude 3,000 m; focal length 25 cm.

Within 5 km the carriage road from Jerusalem to Jaffa descends, between Saris and the inn of Bab el-Wad (8k), from 704 m to 273 m, without then climbing again, so that with this the elevation of the hill country lying before the mountains to the west has been reached. The ridges that accompany the road in Wadi ‘Ali (1c–10m) represent the descent of the mountains at this point.

Bab el-Wad, “the gate of the valley,” is at the same time the crossing point of the still-important meridional (north–south) road at the foot of the mountains, which can be followed from Beersheba to the Beth-Horon road at the northern boundary of Judaea. The picture shows a part of this road leading south (9k–12a). It appears to have been improved during the war.

For the route of the Ark of God, carried on a cart from Beth-Shemesh to Kiriath-Jearim (2 Samuel 7:1), this line must be regarded as probable, because only here is an easy crossing possible from Wadi es-Sarar to Wadi ‘Ali and then a comparatively convenient ascent to Kiriath-Jearim. Cf. No. 41.

div.title: 39. The Jaffa road in the hill country (el-Atrun, Emmaus). View toward the southwest. V. 695.
div.p: FA 304, No. 105. 3 December 1917, 1:45 p.m.; altitude 3,200 m; focal length 25 cm.

The highest elevation in this region is Ras el-‘Abd, 383 m (12bc); a low point is the lower course of Wadi ‘Ali below el-Atrun (8g), at 199 m. With this valley there later unites Wadi Selman (9i), coming from the northeast, which finally drains the plain of Bet Nuba (11, 12a), once the Valley of Aijalon (Joshua 10:12). At its southern edge still lies Jalo-Aijalon (13b); in the terrain between the two valleys lies ‘Amwas-Emmaus-Nicopolis (9d), 225 m, immediately above the more southerly valley el-Atrun (9f)—once a road fortress, 224 m high—beside it a Trappist monastery (8f), and farther up Der Ejub (15, 16cd), 326 m.

Along this valley runs the carriage road from Jerusalem (17d–12i); it formerly crossed the height north of el-Atrun (11f–9e–6f), but now bypasses it to the south (10g–7f) and, above the valley, takes the direction toward Jaffa (6f–1c).

The carriage road is crossed by a road coming from the Beth-Horon road in the northeast through ‘Amwas (8a–6b–8g), which continues southwestward toward Ashdod (8f–2m) and in doing so climbs over into Wadi el-Chalil (10k–2m), which belongs to the system of Wadi es-Sarar, whereas Wadi ‘Ali and Selman drain toward the ‘Odscha River. A ridge road running parallel to the valley road, beginning behind Kerjet Abu Rosch, leads through Jalo and ‘Amwas back to the line of the carriage road (13b–8d–1d).

For comparison, view the illustration of the Domus boni latronis in Zuallart (1586), reproduced in Ammann, Reise ins Gelobte Land (new edition of 1919), fig. 60, and not entirely correctly explained on p. 218. The old road to Jerusalem and the castle viewed from the north, before which the Emmaus church is placed, have as their background a multitude of small mountains evidently meant to represent the mountains of Judah, but which have nothing in common with the reality visible at el-Atrun = Latronis domus. See Orte und Wege Jesu3, pp. 241ff.

div.title: 40. A village in the hill country (Aijalon-Jalo). View toward the west-southwest. V. 677.
div.p: FA 304, No. 2980. 15 September 1918, 8:30 a.m.; altitude 5,000 m; focal length 50 cm.

The village of Jalo (8h–10i), once the Amorite city Aijalon (Judges 1:35), lies on a narrow hill running north–south (288 m) above Wadi ‘Amir (17e–1d), a side branch of Wadi Selman. Beyond the valley is the ruin mound Tell Koka‘ (11ig), probably the old fortress of the place. West of Jalo is the shallow hollow Challet el-Bijara with the spring Ras el-‘En (10k), below the hill of Schech Isma‘in (11k), which one would like to imagine as the ancient place of sacrifice of Aijalon.

The road coming from Jerusalem arrives through Wadi ‘Amir (from 17e), passes south of Jalo (10i), and then turns west (7m) and north (4m–1k) toward ‘Amwas, 3 km to the west; cf. No. 39. To the same place leads the line running alongside the settlement across the plain (9k–1g); to Bet Nuba, across the plain, leads the northeastern road (5g–2a).

div.title: 41. By the brook Sorek (Zorah, Beth-Shemesh). View toward the north. V. 755.
div.p: FA 304, No. 1948. 16 June 1918, 6 a.m.; altitude 4,200 m; focal length 50 cm.

A morning view in June; the dark fields suggest summer crops. The Valley of Sorek (Judges 16:4) corresponds to Wadi es-Sarar, the lower course of the important valley that drains the wider surroundings of Jerusalem and through which the railway line from Jaffa has climbed to Jerusalem since 1892. The picture shows the valley not far from where it emerges from the hill country, where Wadi en-Ndschil (1d–3f) and Wadi Bulos (10a–17f) enter the main valley from the south, and Wadi el-Metlak (6m–8g) from the north. Its waterless channel (1f–17g) runs through the plain of the well-cultivated valley.

The railway follows the channel at some distance on the south side (from 1f at the top to 17g). ‘Artuf station (9g), with a soldiers' camp, lies diagonally opposite the village of ‘Artuf (5k) and the Jewish colony of the same name (5hi).

High above the valley, which lies at about 200 m above sea level, Sar‘a (15, 16m), Zorah, stands on this side at an elevation of 356 m; it was Samson's home (Judges 13:2). On the far side, at an elevation of only 280 m, are ‘En Schems and Khirbet er-Rmele (12, 13e), the Beth-Shemesh of 1 Samuel 6:12ff., then the boundary of Philistine territory. Besides the roads leading westward through Wadi es-Sarar, note the north–south route that crosses the valley near ‘Artuf (6m–8g–1d) and intersects the carriage road to Jaffa at Bab el-Wad; see No. 38.

div.title: 42. The Maccabean city of Modiin, el-Midje. View toward the southwest. V. 654.
div.p: FA 304, No. 151. 14 December 1917, 1:30 p.m.; altitude 2,700 m; focal length 25 cm.

El-Midje, once Modiin, the home and burial place of the Maccabees (1 Maccabees 2:1; 2:69; 13:25), still lies in the hill country. It is separated from the Beth-Horon road to Lydda, which passes to the south but is not visible, by Wadi el-Melaki (4m–2bc), and is isolated on the north by Wadi el-Khanuk (11k–6f), a branch of Wadi el-Kreka (3e–17c).

Probably more significant as the ancient settlement site than the present village (8k) is the summit of er-Ras to the southeast (10l), at 229 m, with a view of the Mediterranean; compare PJB 1912, pp. 19f. To the northeast, likewise at a high elevation (252 m), is the village of Na‘lin (9, 10a) above Wadi en-Natuf (4a–1b), with substantial olive plantations. The oval area (6bc), probably near Schech er-Rafati, resembles an ancient settlement site.

div.title: 43. At the edge of the coastal plain (Neballat, Bet Nebala). View toward the north. V. 155.
div.p: FA 304, No. 137. 13 December 1917, 3:30 p.m.; altitude 2,500 m; focal length 25 cm.

Northwest of el-Midje, immediately beside the coastal plain and near a road that runs northwestward, connecting the Beth-Horon road with the north–south road of the coastal region, lies Bet Nebala (7, 8de), formerly Neballat (Nehemiah 11:34), at an elevation of only 79 m. Two branches of Wadi Kreka (4c and 1k–14e) cut through its extensive olive plantations. A road from ‘Abud to Lidd (1g–15b) passes it on the way to the plain, where the limestone hills (Senonian) abruptly disappear.

div.title: 44. A city in the coastal plain (er-Ramle). View toward the southeast. V. 184.
div.p: FA 304, No. 613. 6 March 1918, 8:15 a.m.; altitude 4,500 m; focal length 25 cm.

In ancient times Lod-Lydda, today Lidd, at an elevation of 58 m, was the center of the coastal region around Jaffa. It has now been surpassed by er-Ramle (9–11d-f), 3 km southwest of it, which can hardly have been Arimathea and first appears in the seventh century AD. The “White Mosque,” with Baibars's tower of 1268, stands to the west, outside the present city (8bc). A large area of orchards lies to the west. The gardens to the north and east belong to Lidd, and the heads of the valleys to the east belong to Wadi Lidd.

The Jerusalem–Jaffa carriage road (13m–11a) skirts the city on the northeast. The railway (12m–17e) crosses the carriage road, reaches its station (12g), and then bends northeast. The carriage road to Lidd (12f–17c), which is later crossed by the railway, indicates precisely the direction in which that city lies. A western and a southwestern road (1a, 1f) lead to Gaza, and a southern road (1m) to Bet Dschibrin.

The Jaffa–Jerusalem road built by ‘Abd al-Malik around 700, which mostly corresponds to the present carriage road (plates 1, 2, 11, 30, 38, 68), was undoubtedly the cause of er-Ramle's rise. It diminished the importance of the Beth-Horon road, along whose route toward Jaffa Lidd lies, and certainly completely replaced the Roman road that approached the same destination through Kerijet Abu Rosch, Jalo, ‘Amwas, and Lidd. In this way ancient Lidd acquired a powerful rival in young er-Ramle.

div.title: C. Samaria and Galilee.
45. The Plain of Jezreel I: view toward the west. V. 1248.
div.p: FA 304, probably December 1917 (see Plain of Jezreel IV); morning.

The Plain of Jezreel marks the separation of northern Palestine from central and southern Palestine. This division was created by a transverse fault running from southeast to northwest and made Galilee a distinct region.

At the same time, the plain forms a natural connection between the coast and the Jordan Valley and serves as one of the country's granaries. It has also been a theater of military campaigns from the time of Deborah and Barak (Judges 4–5) to Napoleon and the recent World War.
The view is taken from the eastern edge of the plain near el-Fule, perhaps the Cyamon of Judith 7:3, at the end of the Assyrian encampment around Bethulia. It is now the Jewish colony of Merchabia.

In the foreground is a farmstead belonging to el-Fule (7–12g). In the middle distance (14f) stands the village of el-‘Afule. Behind it, the Nahr el-Mukatta, the Kishon, begins its course toward the Mediterranean in a channel that is usually dry here.

The hills in the background form the northern edge of the Samaritan highlands, here called Bilad er-Roha. Their most prominent heights are Umm el-Harite (6, 7f), at 312 m, and Umm el-Fahm (3, 4f), at 393 m.
Between these heights, the pass of ‘Ara opens toward the coastal region. At its outlet, probably at 10f, lies Tell el-Mutesellim, Megiddo; compare PJB 1914, pp. 34ff., 76ff.

A dark line behind the farmstead in the foreground (17fg–1g) marks the newest route across the plain, the Haifa–Damascus railway. It is crossed by a second line, the old Nazareth–Jerusalem road (17g–1f), while the new carriage road does not turn south until immediately before el-‘Afule.

div.title: 46. The Plain of Jezreel II: view toward the northwest. V. 1252.
div.p: Morning photograph.
A two-centimeter strip from the right edge of view I is repeated here at the left.

In the foreground is the road from el-Fule to el-‘Afule railway station, with its group of houses (3–7e). Behind it rises the Carmel range. El-Muhraka (4e), at 514 m, is one of the range's highest summits as seen from this direction and is the presumed site of Elijah's sacrifice; compare PJB 1914, pp. 37f., and 1922/23, pp. 24f., 26f.

At the foot of Carmel, whose northwestern end remains out of sight, the Kishon finds its way to the sea. Low, oak-covered hills (10–17e), containing the German colonies of Waldheim and Bethlehem, close off the plain.
From the photographer's position near el-Fule, at an elevation of 78 m, however, a narrow strip of the sea may be visible at 10–11e. The rising hill country on the right already belongs to Galilee.
In the center of the picture (17f–1g) runs the old road from Nazareth to Jerusalem.

div.title: 47. The Plain of Jezreel III: view toward the north-northwest. V. 1253.
div.p: Morning photograph.
A three-centimeter strip of plate 46 is repeated here.

The first tier of the Galilean hill country rises opposite. Its highest point is en-Nebi Sa‘in near Nazareth (14e), at 488 m, which appears lower than Jebel el-Kafze, the “Mount of Precipitation,” at 392 m on the edge of the plain (15e).

Besides elevated Nazareth, en-Nasira (14e), Jafa (10, 11e) is clearly recognizable. Less certain are lower-lying Jinjir, at 136 m near 8f; above it, el-Mujedil, at 238 m; and farther on, probably Ikhnefis (5f) and Jebata (4, 5f).

All the pictures show the fertile plain, the site of intensive grain cultivation, lying bare, which accords with a photograph taken in December. Flying Detachment 304 celebrated Christmas here in 1917.

The outlet of the valley of Nazareth (14ef), the descent of the carriage road from Nazareth to the plain (12ef), and its old continuation across the plain toward Jenin and onward to Jerusalem (11f–1f) can be followed.

div.title: 48. The Plain of Jezreel IV and Jebel ed-Dahi from the west. V. 1253a.
div.p: FA 304, No. 146. 13 December 1917, 3:30 p.m.; focal length 25 cm.
The panorama lacks a view toward the northeast that would show Tabor as the southern end of the Galilean hill country.

Looking east, one sees the final 5 km of the plain before its descent to the Jordan. Because the viewpoint lies between the villages of el-‘Afule and el-Fule, el-Fule itself is visible on its height (8f); below it is the farmstead seen in the foreground of panorama I, and above it (6d) is the summit of Jebel ed-Dahi, at 515 m. This is the (Little) Hermon of Origen and others, but not the Hermon of Psalm 89:13 (Orte und Wege, 3rd ed., pp. 205f.), and perhaps the hill of the oracle-giver in Judges 7:1.
At its southern foot lies Solem (center of 10e), recognizable only as a bright line among its orchards, the Shunem of Elisha (2 Kings 4:8ff.).

The plain rises eastward to 123 m at Jezreel, now Zer‘in, though the right edge of the picture does not extend that far. The mountain wall in the background, only faintly distinguished from the edge of the plain (15–17e), belongs to the region of ‘Ajlun beyond the Jordan. The isolated summit on this side (13e) is Kokab el-Hawa, probably named after Agrippina, the wife of Claudius (PJB 1922/23, pp. 43f.).
